Burial chamber mausoleum. A family mausoleum consisting of six (6) or less casket placement crypts plus a chamber to be used for loading of caskets from the interior of the mausoleum which is not below the level of the ground and which is placed on the same foundation as it rest of the mausoleum, all of which is substantially exposed above the ground.
Chapel mausoleum. A mausoleum for the public that has heat or air conditioning, with or without a committal area or office.
Columbarium. A permanent structure consisting of niches.
Companion crypt. A permanent chamber in a mausoleum for the containment of human remains of more than one (1) individual.
Crypt. A permanent chamber in a mausoleum for the containment of human remains.
Garden mausoleum. A mausoleum for the public built without heat or air conditioning but that may contain an open-air committal area.
Family mausoleum. A mausoleum for the private use of a family or group of family members.
Mausoleum. A permanent structure or building, which is substantially exposed above the ground and is intended for the interment, entombment, or inurnment of human remains.
Niche. A permanent chamber in a columbarium or a mausoleum to hold the cremated remains of one or more individuals.
Non-visitation crypt mausoleum. A mausoleum for the public where the crypts are not accessible to the public.
(Ord. No. 2002-33, § 1, 7-15-02)
624:
The provisions of this article shall apply to buildings or structures as defined in section 5-361 as chapel mausoleums, garden mausoleums, non-visitation crypt mausoleums, mausoleums, burial chamber mausoleums, family mausoleums, companion crypts and columbaria. All crypts and niches built after this article becomes effective shall conform to this article.
(Ord. No. 2002-33, § 1, 7-15-02)
625:
The design and construction of mausoleums and columbaria shall comply with all applicable building and construction regulations of the city and the State of Georgia as well as the following standards:
(1) Crypt pressure relief system shall comply with section 5-368.
(2) Niches shall not require pressure relief systems.
(3) The exterior of the mausoleum shall be comprised of the following materials:
a. Facade: All for (4) sides of the structure shall be constructed of granite facing with brass name plates.
b. Cornice: Copper faced.
c. Walkways: Solid brick pavers shall be used on sidewalks leading to and surrounding the base of the structure.
d. Roof and exterior walls: Granite or marble not less than six (6) inches in thickness and a roof with sufficient "overhang" to protect the exterior walls from the elements.
e. Exterior doors and cornices: Copper, bronze or aluminum alloys or any other material or alloy of similar properties.
(4) Landscaping. Installation of eight (8) mature specimen trees, three (3) inch DBH, consisting of either oak, holly or magnolia surrounding the structure to provide shade and to soften the landscape areas.
(5) Bodies. All bodies interred in the mausoleum must actually be dead. One (1) body per crypt, only.
(6) Viewing. No viewable crypts are permitted.
(7) Weather. Weather-tight and resistant to incursions by insects, water and mold.
(8) Interior. Have interiors constructed of granite, marble, slate, sandstone or limestone.
(9) Foundation. Extend below the frost line (i.e. three feet (3'), be of reinforced steel construction and be covered with brick or stone.
(10) Vandalism. Be capable of being secured against entry by vandals or other unauthorized persons.
(11) Walkways. Walkways shall consist of solid brick pavers having a minimum width of four (4) feet and leading to and surrounding the base of the structure. Poured concrete is prohibited.
(12) Height. Be limited to twenty-six (26) feet.
(13) Square footage. Not exceed one thousand eight hundred (1800) square feet in area.
(14) Examination. Be arranged so that any niche or crypt may be readily examined at any time be any person authorized by law to do so.
(15) Sealing. Provide for permanent sealing of each niche or crypt after the placing of any body or remains therein, and in such manner that no fluid or other matter may escape therefrom.
(16) Construction. Be so constructed as to ensure its beauty, durability and permanence, as well as the safety, convenience, comfort and health of community in which it is located, as dictated and determined at the time by modern mausoleum construction and engineering science standards.
(17) Burial or inurnment. It shall be unlawful for any person who buries a corpse in a mausoleum to fail to ensure that the corpse is buried:
a. In a closed coffin or other container made of wood or metal;
b. In a soundly constructed chamber; and
c. In a chamber in which the number of burials has not exceeded the number of burials for which the chamber was designed, and in no event more than two (2) burials per chamber.
A person who buries a corpse in a mausoleum must ensure that as soon as possible after the burial the front of the chamber is sealed with a slab of impervious material and faced with a slab of stone, slate or iron at least six (6) inches in thickness.
(18) Location. All mausoleums and columbaria must be located in a cemetery.
(Ord. No. 2002-33, § 1, 7-15-02)

635:
As used in this part, the term:
Abandoned well means a well or borehole, the use of which has been permanently discontinued, which is in such a state of disrepair that continued use for obtaining ground water or for other useful purposes is impracticable, or from which ground water for useful purposes is not obtainable.
Administrator means the staff person designated to administer and implement the provisions of this article. The chief building inspector is hereby designated as the "administrator."
Aquifer means a geologic formation, group of formations, or a part of a formation that is capable of yielding water to a well.
Borehole means a hole made into the earth's surface and extending at least fifty (50) feet into the earth or at least ten (10) feet below the water table, whichever is greater, with a drill, auger, or other tool for the purpose of: exploring subsurface strata in search of minerals, engineering or geologic data, water for water supply, blasting purposes, or monitoring.
Business license means an occupation tax certificate issued to a business by a county or municipal government of the state.
Capping or cap means the temporary placing of a watertight seal on the upper terminal of a completed well so that no surface pollutants can enter the well.
Casing means an impervious durable pipe placed in a well to prevent the walls from caving and to seal off surface drainage or undesirable water, gas, or other fluids to prevent them from entering the well and includes specifically, but is not limited to, the following:
(1) Liner pipe which shall mean a well casing installed without driving a protective casing or open drill hole;
(2) Protective casing which shall mean the permanent casing of the well; and
(3) Temporary casing which shall mean a temporary casing placed in soft, sandy, or caving subsurface formations to prevent the hole from caving during drilling.
Construction means all acts necessary to construct a well or borehole for any intended purpose or use, including locating and drilling, but excluding the installation of pumps and pumping equipment.
Contaminant means any physical, chemical, biological, or radiological substance or matter in water, in excess of naturally occurring levels.
Containment device means a device that is designed to contain an unauthorized release of a hazardous material, retain it for cleanup, and prevent released materials from penetrating into the ground.
Continuous transit means the nonstop movement of a vehicle.
Corehole means a borehole made into the earth's surface and extending at least fifty (50) feet into the earth or at least ten (10) feet below the water table, whichever is greater, with a hollow drill to sample a cylindrical section of the earth's strata beneath the surface of the land or water.
Council means the State Water Well Standards Advisory Council.
County health department means, as applicable, either the Clayton County Health Department or the Fulton County Health Department.
Dewatering well means any well withdrawing one hundred thousand (100,000) gallons of ground water or less on any one (1) day in order to remove ground water from the vicinity of an excavation and which extends at least fifty (50) feet into the earth or at least ten (10) feet below the water table, whichever is greater.
Director means the Director of the Environmental Protection Division of the Department of Natural Resources, State of Georgia, or his designee.
Division or GEPD means the Environmental Protection Division of the Department of Natural Resources, State of Georgia.
Driller means any person who engages in drilling or drilling operations.
Drilling or drilling operation means creating an excavation, well, borehole, or corehole by coring, boring, jetting, digging, driving, or otherwise constructing for any intended purpose or use, including locating, testing, or withdrawing ground water which is intended or usable as a source of water supply.
Engineering borehole means a borehole for which the primary purpose is to collect data for engineering design.
Filled, sealed, and plugged means the placing of impervious material when appropriate in the well or borehole to prevent pollutants from entering the subsurface strata or water-bearing formations from the surface, to conserve the aquifer yield or artesian head, or to eliminate physical hazards.
Geologic borehole means any borehole not regulated under the authority of O.C.G.A., Tit. 12, Ch. 4, Art. 2, Pt. 2 for which the primary purpose is to collect data for geologic, geophysical, or mineral resource evaluations.
Ground water means water of underground streams, channels, artesian basins, reservoirs, lakes, and other water under the surface of the earth, whether public or private, natural or artificial, which is contained within, flows through, or borders upon this state or any portion thereof, including those portions of the Atlantic Ocean over which the state has jurisdiction.
Hazardous waste or hazardous material means any waste or material which because of its quantity, concentration, or physical, chemical, or infectious characteristics may:
(1) Cause or significantly contribute to an increase in mortality or an increase in serious irreversible or incapacitating reversible illness; or
(2) Pose a substantial present or potential hazard to human health or to the environment when improperly treated, stored, transported, disposed, or otherwise managed.
Individual water well means any well constructed for the purpose of obtaining ground water to supply water appurtenant to a single-family dwelling and intended for domestic use, including, but not limited to, household purposes, farm livestock, or gardens.
Industrial well means any well constructed for the purpose of withdrawing one hundred thousand (100,000) gallons of ground water or less on any one (1) day for processing or cooling water or for purposes other than drinking water.
Inorganic contaminants means compounds that do not contain carbon, e.g., nitrogen and phosphorus nutrients, heavy metals, sodium, and chloride.
Irrigation well means any well constructed for the purpose of obtaining ground water to supply irrigation water for agriculture, silviculture, golf courses, fish farms, and land beautification, but excluding single-family irrigation of lawns or gardens.
Irrigation well, residential means any well constructed for the purpose of obtaining ground water to supply irrigation water for residential irrigation of lawns or gardens but not for human consumption or domestic household use. Residential irrigation wells are normally shallow wells of less than one hundred (100) feet depth.
Monitoring well means any well for which the primary purpose is to collect data for hydrologic, geohydrologic, or ground water quality or quantity evaluations.
Nonpublic water well means any well constructed as a source of potable water supply for a water system which provides piped water to the public for human consumption, if such system has less than fifteen (15) service connections or regularly serves less than twenty-five (25) individuals, excluding individual water wells.
Organic compounds means any molecules containing carbon, e.g., petroleum-based and hydrocarbon-based products, PCBs, pesticides, and other volatile and semi-volatile compounds such as benzene, napthalenes and phenols.
Owner means the legal owner of the land upon which the well is being excavated.
Person means any individual, partnership, association, trust, firm, corporation, county, municipality, or other entity, including the state and the federal government.
Pollutant means dredged spoil, solid waste, incinerator residue, sewage, garbage, sewage sludge, munitions, chemical wastes, biological materials, radioactive materials, heat, wrecked or discarded equipment, rock, sand, cellar dirt, industrial wastes, municipal wastes, agricultural wastes, or any other wastes or substances that do not naturally occur in the aquifer.
Potable water supply means any water used or intended to be used for drinking, bathing, culinary, or other personal purposes.
Professional engineer means a person registered to practice professional engineering in the State of Georgia in accordance with O.C.G.A., Tit. 43, Ch. 15.
Professional geologist means a person registered to practice as a geologist in the State of Georgia in accordance with O.C.G.A., Tit. 43, Ch. 19.
Public water system means a system that provides piped water for human consumption, if such system has at least fifteen (15) service connections or regularly serves an average of at least twenty-five (25) individuals daily at least sixty (60) days out of the year. Such term includes: (1) any collection, treatment, storage, and distribution facilities under control of the operator of such system and used primarily in connection with such system, and (2) any collection or pretreatment storage facilities not under such control which are used primarily in connection with such system. A public water system is either a "community water system" or a "non-community water system."
(1) Community water system means a public water system which serves at least fifteen (15) service connections used by year round residents or regularly serves at least twenty-five (25) year-round residents.
(2) Non-community water system means a public water system that is not a community water system. Some non-community water systems may be further classified as "nontransient, non-community water systems."
(3) Non-transient, non-community water system means a public water system that is not a community water system and that regularly serves at least twenty-five (25) of the same people over six (6) months per year.
Public water system wellhead protection zone means the surface and subsurface area surrounding water well or well field supplying a potable public water system, through which contaminants are reasonably likely to move toward and reach such well or well field.
Sanitary landfill means a disposal site where solid wastes, including putrescible wastes or hazardous wastes, are disposed on land by placing earth cover thereon.
Seismic shot hole means any borehole in which explosives are detonated for the purpose of seismic investigations.
Storm water drainage means a storm water main or other system for conveying surface runoff due to storm events and unpolluted groundwater or surface water, including that collected by cellar drains but excluding sanitary sewage and industrial waste.
Surface runoff means that part of the precipitation that passes over the surface of the soil to the nearest surface stream without first passing beneath the surface.
Viral or bacterial contaminants means microscopic organisms harmful to human health, e.g., pathogens.
Wastewater means any combination of water-carried wastes from residential, institutional, commercial, or industrial establishments, including any stormwater, surface water, or groundwater as may be present.
Under the direction of a professional geologist or professional engineer means that a professional geologist or professional engineer has reviewed well or borehole drilling, construction, and abandonment plans or criteria and has provided instructions to the driller as to how the well or borehole is to be drilled, constructed, or abandoned.
Water table means, exclusive of perched conditions, the shallowest permanent occurrence of ground water.
Water well means any excavation which is cored, bored, drilled, jetted, dug, or otherwise constructed for the purpose of locating, testing, or withdrawing ground water and which is intended or usable as a source of water supply for individual homes, farms, irrigation, industrial processes, public water systems, or nonpublic water systems.
Water well contractor means any person engaging in the business of constructing water wells.
Well means any excavation in which the vertical dimension exceeds the horizontal dimension that is bored, cored, drilled, dug, jetted, or otherwise constructed for the purpose of locating, testing, or withdrawing ground water; or for evaluating, testing, developing, draining, or recharging ground water reservoirs or aquifers; or for the exploration, evaluating, testing, or developing of minerals; or which causes the movement of water from or into any aquifer or subsurface strata; and shall include engineering and geologic boreholes.
Well field means a tract of land that contains more than one (1) existing or proposed well for supplying water.
Wellhead means the upper terminal of a well, including adaptors, ports, seals, valves, and other attachments and any structure built over or extending over a well.
(Ord. No. 2010-26, § 1, 11-15-10)

653:
There is hereby established the College Park Commercial Leasing Relations Commission ("Commission"), which shall serve in an advisory capacity to the city council and city manager. The purpose of the commission is to strengthen communication, transparency, and collaboration between commercial tenants and commercial property owners within the City of College Park.
The city recognizes that commercial tenants contribute significantly to the city's economic vitality and that productive relationships between tenants and property owners are essential to business stability, corridor revitalization, and local economic development. The commission is established to identify challenges associated with commercial leasing, promote fair and responsible commercial leasing practices, support communication among stakeholders, and provide recommendations that advance a strong and sustainable commercial environment.
(Ord. No. 2025-26, § 1(Exh. A), 12-1-25)
654:
The commission shall have the following powers and responsibilities:
(1) Advisory role. Advise the city council, city manager, economic development department on issues affecting commercial tenants and property owners, including maintenance, leasing practices, code compliance, redevelopment impacts, and business retention factors.
(2) Policy recommendations. Recommend legislative or administrative strategies to improve commercial leasing conditions, strengthen communication, and support equitable, stable, and economically healthy commercial corridors to the city council.
(3) Stakeholder engagement. Facilitate engagement with commercial tenants, property owners, and other stakeholders by organizing listening sessions, gathering public input, and promoting awareness of city programs, permitting processes, and commercial-leasing best practices.
(4) Research and monitoring. Collect and analyze information regarding commercial leasing trends, common issues, corridor-specific challenges, and systemic concerns affecting business operations. Provide findings and data-supported recommendations to the city council on a quarterly basis.
(5) Interagency collaboration. Coordinate with other city boards, commissions, and departments on matters where commercial leasing intersects with zoning, economic development, public safety, transportation, infrastructure, or redevelopment.
(6) Regulatory awareness. Support public awareness of applicable city codes, building standards, property maintenance requirements, and relevant state law governing commercial leasing and business operations.
(7) Support for commercial tenants. Promote awareness of available resources, informational materials, and business-support programs that assist commercial tenants in understanding their rights, responsibilities, and available remedies under local and state law.
(8) Bylaws. The commission may adopt bylaws consistent with this article and applicable law, which shall become effective upon approval by the city manager or designee. A current copy of the bylaws shall be maintained with the city clerk.
(Ord. No. 2025-26, § 1(Exh. A), 12-1-25)
656:
(a) Composition. The commission shall be composed of five (5) voting members, appointed as follows: (i) Two (2) commercial tenant members, each of whom operates a business within a leased commercial space located inside the City of College Park; (ii) two (2) Commercial Property Owner members, each of whom owns commercial property within the City of College Park; and (iii) one (1) at-large member with professional experience in commercial real estate, business operations, economic development, commercial property law, or related subject-matter expertise.
(b) Appointment of voting members. Each member of the governing body shall appoint one (1) voting member to the commission; provided, however, that all appointments must collectively comply with the membership composition requirements set forth in subsection (a). In making appointments, members of the governing body shall consider the diversity of business types, geographic areas, commercial corridors, and economic sectors represented within the city.
(c) Non-voting advisory members. The city council may, by majority vote, appoint up to two (2) non-voting advisory members. Advisory members may include, but are not limited to, commercial real estate professionals, attorneys, property managers, business-association representatives, chamber of commerce participants, or other individuals with relevant expertise. Advisory members may participate fully in deliberations but shall not vote on commission actions.
(d) Term. Members shall serve staggered four (4) year terms. Initial appointments may be adjusted to establish staggered term cycles. Any member who ceases to meet the qualification criteria for their appointed category shall be deemed to have vacated the position.
